title: No beings freed (section 25)
hook: the Tathagata doesn't think "I free beings"; there are no beings for him to free

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaps of jewels piled high as mountains, and four lines kept by heart outweighed them all. Your line: less than four lines.

Two neighbors shovel the same snowy sidewalk for an old man down the street. One does it before dawn and never brings it up. The other brings it up at every barbecue for a year. Same snow, same clear path. But the second one carries something extra home: a little ledger. I did that. For him. He owes me. Section twenty-five of the Diamond Sutra goes after that ledger at the very top, with the Tathagata, the awakened one himself.
screen: `SAME SNOW, TWO SHOVELERS.` → `ONE KEEPS A LEDGER.` → `DOES THE BUDDHA KEEP ONE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: does the Tathagata think, I have set beings free? Don't think so, Subhuti. That's a strange thing to deny, since the sutra opened with a vow to free all beings. The reason: there is no being whom the Tathagata has set free. If he thought that way, he'd be holding on to an idea of a self, a being, a living soul, a person, the same four ideas the sutra has been cutting since section three. Notice what goes and what stays. The help doesn't vanish. The helper's tally does. Then a turn the sutra loves. What is called a self is taught by the Tathagata as no self, and yet ordinary, unlearned people hold on to it. And those ordinary people are not ordinary people either; they're only called that. Nobody is written off as hopeless, not even the person still clinging. The label gets cut along with the self. In section three, the bodhisattva vowed to lead all beings to nirvana while knowing that no being is led. Section twenty-five points that same vow at the Tathagata. Even at the very top, the rule holds. Way back on day one hundred thirty-seven, you met giving without a receipt; here it is, all the way up. Some Mahayana teachers describe a gift as clean when the giver, the gift and the one who receives are all held lightly. A help that keeps no ledger has nothing to collect, and nobody is left owing.
screen: `DOES HE THINK "I FREE BEINGS"?` · `NO BEING TO FREE.` · `SELF IS TAUGHT AS NO SELF.` · `HELP WITHOUT A LEDGER.` · then, large: `NO ONE TO FREE.`

segments.voice: Call to mind one small thing you could do for someone: a text, a dish washed, a door held. Notice the little voice already taking notes, they'll remember this, and let it go quiet. See the help as just the next thing that needs doing, the way a hand brushes crumbs off a table, and rest with the breath.
No beings freed. Section twenty-five: the Tathagata doesn't think, I have set beings free, because there's no being he holds on to as freed. Today's word.
Your line: no one to free. The help stays; only the tally goes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that study the Diamond Sutra, section 25 is read with the bodhisattva vow from section 3: beings are helped without the helper holding on to the thought "I freed them."

chat.says: If the Buddha frees beings, why does the Diamond Sutra say he doesn't think 'I freed them'?
options: He still helps; he just doesn't hold that thought, which would bring back an idea of a self.
In the sutra the Buddha decides that helping others is a distraction from awakening.
Only beings who ask him directly are freed, so most beings are never freed.
chat.meaning: Section twenty-five keeps the help and drops the helper's tally: thinking 'I freed beings' would mean holding an idea of a self.

Tathagata.meaning: the awakened one; a title the Buddha uses for himself

Subhuti.meaning: the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra

Diamond Sutra.meaning: a short Mahayana sutra that cuts through every grip

bodhisattva.meaning: one who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings
